newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-HOLYFIELD NOT RULED OUT CHARGES AGAINST TYSON.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-HOLYFIELD NOT RULED OUT CHARGES AGAINST TYSON.

text.p: World heavyweight champion Evander Holyfield has not ruled out filing charges against Mike Tyson for biting off part of his ear during their title bout, Holyfield's attorney said on Sunday.

"We have not discussed filing criminal charges," Jim Thomas told reporters. The lawyer said he believed Tyson's actions in the ring on Saturday night were "tortious" -- suggesting the champion might pursue a civil suit.
"Whether we do anything about it, we will decide in due course," he told reporters.
Thomas said the devoutly Christian Holyfield "is not a vengeful person, he is kind-hearted and would be the first to forgive."
However, he added, "here's a guy who caused a lot of pain to a lot of people all round and we're not sitting around thinking about 'poor Mike Tyson'."

During the unprecedented melee that erupted in the ring after Tyson was disqualified at the end of the third round, Tyson was seen swinging at a police officer trying to restrain him from getting to Holyfield.
Las Vegas police had no immediate comment on whether they would take action. If charged with assault, Tyson could be in violation of his parole following his jail term for rape.
Tyson was roundly condemned on Sunday for twice biting Holyfield in their World Boxing Association title rematch.
After losing the first two rounds, Tyson came out in the third without his mouthguard and was told to put it in. Then in a clinch he tore out a chunk of the champion's right ear.
Thomas said doctors were unable to re-attach the piece of flesh, some 3/4-inch by 1/4-inch.

"The piece torn away could not be re-attached and Holyfield will have to undergo reconstructive plastic surgery," he said. Holyfield's left ear was "pretty much bitten through, but there's nothing missing," he added.
Thomas said Holyfield was in pain and taking medication.

Tyson was in seclusion on Sunday, temporarily suspended from boxing by the Nevada State Athletic Commission, which also withheld his $30 million purse. The Commission will meet on Tuesday to decide what action to take.
Holyfield's lawyer was blunt in his opinion.

"For the good of this sport there needs to be some consequences," Thomas said, without specifying whether he wanted Tyson fined or banned from boxing. "If someone can do what we all saw in the ring with our own eyes, it will be negative for boxing."
He said Holyfield "got angry because it was completely out of bounds and disrespectful of the sport."
The attorney said it was likely the champion would fight again this year -- but not against Tyson, whom he beat last November when the referee stopped the bout in the 11th round.
"We don't believe Mike Tyson deserves to be in the ring with Evander Holyfield now," he said.
Asked whether Tyson's biting was triggered by a head-butt in the second round that referee Mills Lane said was unintentional, Thomas launched into a diatribe against Tyson.

"Tyson leads with his head and with two fighters like that a clash of heads is inevitable. But biting ears is not inevitable. It is sad, if not pathetic, that Tyson makes excuses for inexcusable behaviour," he said.

Holyfield's trainer Don Turner earlier told reporters he felt his fighter's aggressive start to Saturday's fight, in which he caught Tyson with a sharp right to the head in the first round, set Tyson off.
"I think Holyfield would have knocked Tyson out -- in the first round he almost did, and that set the tone for what happened."

Turner said he did not want a rematch, nor did he believe Tyson should be banned from boxing. Rather, he decried the attitude of a man who at 20 was the youngest world heavyweight champion, but whose personal life has been in turmoil.
"He was bad as a kid, then bad as a fighter -- nothing has changed," said the veteran trainer.
"I was saddened by the events. It was supposed to be the greatest event in professional sports but was marred by the fights -- it was just ugly."
